title: Cooperative Societies and Joint Stock Companies
meta: Lesson practice set · Question types of the April 2026 NIOS paper
instructions: Practice set for this lesson in the question types of the April 2026 paper.
Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.answer: A

questions.answer: B

questions.answer: D

questions.answer: D

questions.q: The minimum number of members to form a public company is —
questions.answer: B

questions.q: The primary aim of a cooperative society is to —
questions.answer: B

questions.answer: C

questions.answer: C

questions.answer: B

questions.answer: C

questions.answer: D

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or identify).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Indian Oil Corporation and ONGC are examples of ________. (b) The risk of loss in a company is spread over a large number of ________.
questions.answer:
(a) government companies
(b) shareholders

questions.q: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Death, bankruptcy or insanity of members does not affect the continuity of a cooperative society. (b) A cooperative society can be started with a minimum of 2 members.
questions.answer:
(a) True — it has a separate legal entity and stable life.
(b) False — it needs at least 10 members.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The minimum paid-up capital to start a private limited company was ₹ ________. (b) The liability of the members of a cooperative society is ________.
questions.answer:
(a) 1 lakh (under the Companies Act, 1956; the 2013 Act as amended has no minimum)
(b) limited

questions.q: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) Domestic producers improve the quality of their products because of multinational companies. (b) It is necessary to get every company incorporated, whether private or public.
questions.answer:
(a) True — competition from MNCs pushes them to improve.
(b) True — registration under the Companies Act is compulsory.

questions.q: Mrs. Reeta is afraid that if her business assets fall short, her personal assets may be used to pay the debts. (a) Which form of organisation should she choose? (b) Why?
questions.answer:
(a) A joint stock company.
(b) Its shareholders have limited liability — they lose at most the value of their shares; personal assets are safe.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: 'Members may come and members may go, but the company continues to exist.' Identify and explain this feature of a joint stock company.
questions.answer: Perpetual succession. A company is a separate legal entity created by law, so its life is not affected by the death, insolvency, retirement or transfer of shares of any member. It ends only when it is wound up by law.

questions.q: State any two features of a government company.
questions.answer:
(1) At least 51% of its paid-up share capital is held by the central or state government.
(2) It is registered under the Companies Act and has a separate legal entity; its directors are mostly appointed by the government and its accounts are audited under the CAG.

questions.q: State two disadvantages of a joint stock company.
questions.answer:
(1) Difficult and expensive formation with many legal formalities.
(2) Lack of secrecy — accounts must be published.
(Also: delay in decisions; separation of ownership and control may lead to misuse.)

or.q: State two disadvantages of a multinational company.
or.answer:
(1) They may harm small domestic industries that cannot compete.
(2) They send large profits to their home country, causing an outflow of foreign exchange.
(Also: exploitation of natural resources; interference in local affairs.)

questions.q: What is a thrift and credit cooperative society? Explain.
questions.answer: It is a cooperative formed to give financial help to its members. It collects small savings (thrift) from members as deposits and lends money to members in need at low rates of interest, saving them from moneylenders. Examples: village service cooperative societies, urban cooperative banks.

questions.q: Explain any two features of cooperative societies.
questions.answer:
(1) Voluntary and open membership — anyone with a common interest can join or leave freely.
(2) Democratic management — 'one man, one vote', whatever the number of shares held.
(Also: compulsory registration, limited liability, service motive, stable life.)

questions.q: Vinod wants a business in which his personal assets cannot be used to pay business debts. Suggest a form. OR A cooperative set up in Chandigarh gives members houses and civic amenities at low cost. Identify its type.
questions.answer:
Vinod: a joint stock company, whose members have limited liability.
The Chandigarh society is a cooperative (group) housing society.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: State any three limitations of a cooperative society.
questions.answer:
(1) Limited capital — members are usually of small means and get only a limited dividend.
(2) Inefficient management — honorary office-bearers may lack business skill.
(3) Lack of motivation and conflicts among members; excessive government control. (Any three.)

questions.q: State any three limitations of a joint stock company.
questions.answer:
(1) Difficult and costly formation.
(2) Excessive government regulation and lack of secrecy.
(3) Delay in decision-making and possible misuse of power by directors because ownership is separate from management. (Any three.)

questions.q: What is meant by a private company? State three of its features.
questions.answer:
A company that restricts the transfer of its shares and does not invite the public to buy them.
(1) Minimum 2 and maximum 200 members (50 under the old Act).
(2) Restriction on transfer of shares.
(3) Cannot issue a prospectus; needs at least 2 directors and can start business on getting the certificate of incorporation.

questions.q: Joint stock company: explain (a) perpetual succession (b) separation of ownership and management.
questions.answer:
(a) Perpetual succession: the company has its own existence; the death, insolvency or exit of members does not affect it.
(b) Separation of ownership and management: shareholders own the company but, being many and scattered, they elect a board of directors who manage it.

questions.q: Why do members of a cooperative society not work with full zeal? Explain along with other limitations.
questions.answer:
Members get only a limited dividend on capital and no extra reward for extra effort, and office-bearers are often honorary — so there is little personal motivation.
Other limitations: limited capital; inefficient management; conflicts among members; excessive government control; lack of secrecy.

sections.title: Long answer questions, including case-based questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Amul is an Indian dairy cooperative formed in 1946 and owned by 3.6 million producers in Gujarat; it led India's white revolution. (a) What is a cooperative society? (b) Why was Amul promoted as a cooperative? Explain four merits of the cooperative form.
questions.answer:
(a) A cooperative society is a voluntary association of persons who join together on the basis of equality to promote their common economic interest, with service to members as its main aim.
(b) Small milk producers could not sell profitably alone and were exploited by middlemen; together they could collect, process and market milk themselves. Merits:
(1) Elimination of middlemen — producers get a fair price.
(2) Democratic management — one man, one vote, so every producer has a say.
(3) Limited liability and stable life — unaffected by death or exit of members.
(4) Government support and easy formation; service at low cost to members.

questions.q: What are multinational companies? Give two examples and explain any four advantages.
questions.answer:
A multinational company has its head office in one country and operates factories or offices in several other countries. Examples: Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Samsung, Coca-Cola.
(1) Inflow of foreign capital into the host country.
(2) Latest technology and research.
(3) Employment opportunities.
(4) Better quality goods and wider choice for consumers; competition improves domestic products.
(5) Export promotion and foreign exchange earnings.

questions.q: Explain any three advantages and two limitations of joint stock companies.
questions.answer:
Advantages: (1) Large capital from many shareholders. (2) Limited liability encourages investment. (3) Perpetual succession and transferability of shares; professional management.
Limitations: (1) Difficult, costly formation and excessive legal control. (2) Delay in decisions and lack of secrecy.

questions.q: Distinguish between a private limited and a public limited company on any five bases.
questions.answer:
Minimum members: 2 vs 7.
Maximum members: 200 (50 earlier) vs no limit.
Transfer of shares: restricted vs free.
Prospectus: cannot invite the public vs can issue a prospectus.
Directors: at least 2 vs at least 3.
Commencement of business: on incorporation vs (earlier) after a certificate of commencement.

questions.q: What is a joint stock company? Explain any four of its characteristics.
questions.answer:
A voluntary association of persons formed under the Companies Act with capital divided into transferable shares.
(1) Artificial legal person and separate legal entity.
(2) Perpetual succession.
(3) Limited liability of shareholders.
(4) Transferability of shares.
(5) Separation of ownership and management; common seal; compulsory registration.

questions.q: What are the activities of a consumers' cooperative society? Explain four features of cooperative societies.
questions.answer:
A consumers' cooperative buys goods in bulk directly from producers or wholesalers and sells them to members (and others) at reasonable prices, removing middlemen; profit is shared as a bonus on purchases. Examples: Kendriya Bhandar, Apna Bazar.
Features: (1) voluntary, open membership; (2) compulsory registration with at least ten members; (3) democratic control — one man, one vote; (4) service motive; also limited liability and separate legal entity.
